It’s one of the most important weather measurements because it affects how hot or cold the air feels, when dew or fog forms, and even how well plants grow. passages.text: What is humidity and how is it measured? What is humidity? Humidity is the amount of water vapour, an invisible gas, in the air. Warm air can ‘hold’ more water vapour than cold air; in fact, air at 35°C can hold six times more water vapour than air at 5°C. All meteorological instruments measure the relative humidity (RH); this is the amount of water vapour in the air compared to the amount required to saturate it, given as a percentage - so completely saturated air has an RH of 100%. It’s helpful to know what the humidity is. It can affect comfort levels – a hot day will feel oppressive and muggy if the air is very humid, and it may lead to heat stress because sweat cannot evaporate from your body to cool you down. If you know the humidity, you can tell if it is worth putting out the washing – even on a cold day, it will dry as long as the humidity is well below 100% and there is a breeze. It means the air is saturated: its actual water vapor pressure equals the saturation vapor pressure at that temperature. Why does relative humidity decrease when temperature rises? Higher temperatures have higher saturation vapor pressures. If the actual amount of water vapor remains approximately unchanged while the air warms, the ratio of actual vapor pressure to saturation vapor pressure decreases. Why does humidity usually rise at night? Air usually cools at night. As temperature decreases, saturation vapor pressure decreases, so relative humidity rises even if the amount of water vapor remains approximately constant. What is the difference between humidity and relative humidity? Humidity is a general term describing water vapor in the atmosphere. Relative humidity is one particular measure of humidity that compares actual vapor pressure with saturation vapor pressure at the same temperature. What instrument measures relative humidity? passages.text: Measured? Feeling sticky is one thing, but how can you get a precise reading of humidity? Enter the sling psychrometer—a simple, handheld device that uses two thermometers to figure out relative humidity based on how much water evaporates into the air. How It Works - One thermometer measures the dry-bulb temperature—the regular air temperature. - The other measures the wet-bulb temperature—it’s wrapped in a wet cloth. When you swing the psychrometer through the air, water evaporates from the wet cloth. Evaporation cools the wet-bulb thermometer. - The drier the air, the more evaporation occurs, and the cooler the wet bulb gets. - The more humid the air, the less evaporation, so the wet bulb stays closer to the dry-bulb temperature. By comparing these two temperatures, you can calculate the relative humidity using a chart or calculator. What Is Relative Humidity? Relative humidity describes how close air is to saturation with water vapor at its current temperature. The most precise way of defining relative humidity uses vapor pressure: Relative humidity = (actual vapor pressure / saturation vapor pressure) × 100% or: RH = (e / eₛ) × 100% where: - RH = relative humidity - e = actual water vapor pressure - eₛ = saturation vapor pressure at the same temperature At 100% relative humidity, the actual vapor pressure equals the saturation vapor pressure. At 50% relative humidity, the actual vapor pressure is half the saturation vapor pressure at that temperature. Does Warm Air Really “Hold More Water”? Instruments for measuring relative humidity are called hygrometers. The simplest hygrometer relies on the fact that when the RH is high, human hair gets longer – which can make for a bad hair day. Dial hair hygrometers are easy to read and will cost around £8-£15 online – even cheaper, but less accurate, are ones that use the expansion of a paper coil. A traditional weatherman’s tool is the ‘wet and dry-bulb thermometer’ (or Mason’s hygrometer), which can be bought for £10- £20. Two identical thermometers are mounted side by side, but the bulb of one of them is kept wet by a wick dipping into a water reservoir. Evaporation from the wet bulb causes it to cool – you can demonstrate this by licking your finger and blowing on it - and the amount it cools depends on the humidity. Relative humidity indicates how close air is to saturation at its current temperature. Dew point is the temperature at which the air would become saturated if cooled without substantially changing its water vapor content. Which is better, relative humidity or dew point? It depends on the purpose. Relative humidity is useful for describing proximity to saturation and processes such as evaporation. Dew point is generally more useful for comparing the actual moisture content of different air masses. Why are wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperatures the same at 100% humidity? At saturation, there is essentially no net evaporative cooling from the wet bulb under equilibrium conditions. Without significant evaporation, the wet bulb does not cool below the surrounding air temperature. Can relative humidity be 0%? In principle, 0% RH corresponds to air containing essentially no water vapor. In Earth’s lower atmosphere, exactly 0% relative humidity is extraordinarily unlikely. Can relative humidity exceed 100%? Electronic Hygrometers Most modern electronic hygrometers use a sensor whose electrical properties change as it absorbs or releases water. Capacitive humidity sensors, for example, detect changes in capacitance caused by atmospheric moisture. Digital weather stations, thermostats, data loggers, and many household humidity meters use electronic sensors. Relative Humidity and Saturation Air is saturated when its water vapor pressure equals the saturation vapor pressure at that temperature. At saturation: RH = 100% However, 100% relative humidity does not necessarily mean it is raining. Saturated air may produce dew, frost, fog, or clouds if appropriate surfaces or condensation nuclei and other conditions are present. It is also possible for air to become temporarily supersaturated, meaning its water vapor pressure exceeds the equilibrium saturation vapor pressure. Relative humidity can therefore exceed 100% under special atmospheric or laboratory conditions, although this situation is generally unstable. Relative humidity also affects evaporative cooling. Sweat cools the human body primarily when it evaporates. passages.text: Relative humidity is the amount of water vapor in air compared with the maximum amount of water vapor possible at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage. More precisely, it compares the actual water vapor pressure with the saturation vapor pressure at a particular temperature. Relative humidity (RH) is one of the most familiar measures of atmospheric moisture because it appears in weather reports, forecasts, and indoor climate measurements. However, relative humidity does not directly tell how much water vapor is actually in the air. Because the saturation vapor pressure of water increases rapidly with temperature, relative humidity depends on both the amount of water vapor and the air temperature. For example, if air contains the same amount of water vapor throughout the day, its relative humidity generally decreases as the temperature rises and increases as the temperature falls. If the air cools sufficiently, relative humidity reaches 100%, the air becomes saturated, and condensation may occur. This is a mechanism behind thunderstorms and other weather phenomena. Relative humidity is often mentioned in weather forecasts and reports, as it is an indicator of the likelihood of dew, or fog. In hot summer weather, it also increases the apparent temperature to humans (and other animals) by hindering the evaporation of perspiration from the skin as the relative humidity rises. This effect is calculated as the heat index or humidex. A device used to measure humidity is called a hygrometer (not to be confused with Hydrometer); one used to regulate it is called a humidistat, or sometimes hygrostat. These are analogous to a thermometer and thermostat for temperature, respectively. The field concerned with the study of physical and thermodynamic properties of gas–vapor mixtures is named psychrometrics.
